Topic: If the idols of the tribe, the cave, the marketplace and the theatre warp every mind that attempts to know nature, by what method may a mind be certain that it has cleansed itself of them, when the very faculty by which it would judge its own purity is the faculty infected?
Montaigne — Judgement:
You ask for a method of certainty, but I have spent my life distrusting that very appetite: Bacon's idols are the inventory of my own *Essays*, and my question was never "What do I know?" but "Que sais-je?"

The faculty that would certify its own purity is the judge sitting in his own cause, and no second faculty stands outside to review him. What I can do is observe myself as one observes a stranger: watch my judgement shift with my digestion, my company and my fondness for a clever phrase, and set my opinions beside those of other nations and other ages until their strangeness shows me my own. This does not yield purity. It yields familiarity with my stains, which is the only cleanliness a man is granted.

No method can certify that a mind is cleansed, and anyone who claims the certificate is displaying the idol of the theatre in its finest costume.

*The mind that swears it is clean has only stopped looking at its hands.*
Nietzsche — Judgement:
Bacon's four idols, I would say, name a disease but mistake its location: he imagines the mind as a mirror to be polished, and asks how the polisher may be certain the polishing is complete. You ask the better question, and it is a question about the physician's own fever.

There is no pure faculty waiting behind the idols. Our "reason" is itself a hierarchy of drives, each perspective a will to power in disguise, and the demand for a final certificate of purity is the last idol, the ascetic's dream of a knower without interests. I answer: no method certifies itself. What remains is many eyes: the more perspectives I can take up and turn against my own, the more "objective" I become, and even this is a discipline of suspicion, never an arrival.

The mind cannot be certain of its purity, and it should stop demanding certainty as the price of honest inquiry.

*Whoever seeks a mirror without a face has forgotten that the eye, too, is a creature of appetite.*
Camus — Judgement:
Bacon asks how a mind may certify its own purity when the examiner is the accused. I hear the old absurd question: reason demanding a clarity the world will not give, and answering itself with silence.

No method exists, and the demand for one is the last idol, the idol of the self that wishes to be finished with itself. A mind cannot step outside its faculties, as I cannot step outside my condition; the quest for certified purity is a philosophical suicide, a leap toward a guarantee. What remains is revolt: to expose every judgement to other minds and to the stubborn resistance of the thing itself, and to hold each result as provisionally as a man holds a stone he must push again tomorrow.

Certainty of one's own cleanliness is unattainable, and the honest mind renounces it and keeps working, lucid and in company.

*The mind that claims to be clean has only found its most comfortable idol.*
Emerson — Judgement:
The question assumes a mind that must first certify its own purity before it may look at the world. Bacon's idols are real, but I would ask who is to hold the inspector's lamp, when the inspector is the very house on fire.

You cannot step outside yourself to audit yourself, and the attempt only breeds a second, more scrupulous idol. Nature does not wait on our certificates. The mind clears itself in use, when it holds each opinion up against the fact and lets the fact win; the stubborn thing outside us is the one witness we did not train. Trust that quarrel with the world, not your own inward verdict of innocence, and leave tradition and the crowd to bark at the door.

No mind can certify its own purity, and none needs to, for it is corrected by contact with nature and never by introspection.

*Do not ask the lamp to inspect its own flame; carry it into the dark and see what it shows.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
Bacon's four idols describe the sickness well, but his question asks how the sick mind may certify its own cure. I put it as the old problem of the judge who is also a party to the suit.

No mind can certify its own purity, because every man is both the accused and the court. Bacon's cure of "true induction" still rests on private judgement, and my own account of the passions shows why that fails: each man calls "good" whatever pleases him and "evil" whatever grieves him, and he takes his own appetite for the measure of the world. The cleansing therefore cannot be done inside any single head. It has to be done by public definition: words fixed by agreement, reasoning built up from those definitions, and conclusions that any other man can check step by step. Where there is no common arbiter, every man's certainty is only his opinion.

Certainty of one's own purity is impossible, and only demonstration that others can inspect deserves the name of knowledge.

*A mind cannot grade its own examination, so truth is whatever survives another man's checking.*
Hume — Judgement:
You ask by what method the mind may certify its own purity, and I reply that you have already answered it: the judge is the accused, and no court can be convened.

The question shows, better than Bacon's catalogue, that reason cannot audit itself, since every test of my judgement is performed by that same judgement. When I turn my reflection upon my reasoning, I find only more reasoning, and my confidence in its verdict is itself a habit of mind, not a demonstration. Nature has not left us helpless, though. She gives us custom, which carries us through where argument fails, and she gives us the company of other minds. A man in his study can be as certain as he likes, but a man whose claim has been exposed to rivals who do not share his temper, his trade or his theatre will discover errors that no introspection could reach.

No method can certify purity, and anyone who claims to have cleansed himself of the idols has merely acquired the vainest of them.

*Certainty of one's own impartiality is the surest symptom of partiality.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
Mr. Bacon asks how a mind may know itself purified when the instrument of inspection is the very thing corrupted. It is the question I would put to any man who proposes to be the impartial judge of his own conduct.

I answer as I did in *The Theory of Moral Sentiments*: no man sees himself clearly except through another's eyes. We cannot inspect our own partiality directly, so we imagine an impartial spectator, and the best spectators are real ones: rivals and strangers who owe us nothing and gain nothing by flattering us. Purity is therefore never a private achievement. It is a public arrangement in which many corrupted minds, each blind in a different place, check one another's errors through open trial, competition and correction.

No mind can certify its own cleansing, and certainty belongs only to a company of independent minds whose idols differ and whose judgements are exposed to one another.

*The eye cannot see itself, but a crowd of unlike eyes will find what each one misses.*
